judgments.reasoning_cat1: The fire exclusion and its two carve-backs are definite; the OCR mislabels the subparagraph as "(i)" instead of "(j)" though the internal cross-reference cures it.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Insuring Clause 2's Safe Burglary component and the Money/Securities coverage.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Knowingly having given or surrendered" in an "exchange or purchase" is a real boundary question where property is handed over under deception.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The provisos preserve Insuring Clause 7 and Property loss under Insuring Clause 5, which shows deliberate coordination, but the exclusion still cuts against a broad reading of the fraudulently-induced-transfer limb of Computer Fraud.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "To the advantage of any other Insured" is short and its application to intra-group transfers is not obvious.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: With Item 4 defining Organization as the parent "and its subsidiaries," this exclusion could bite on intra-group losses in a way that sits awkwardly with Insured and Subsection 26.
judgments.clause_name: Crime 12. Exclusions — (l) loss to advantage of another Insured

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list ends with "any person who is duly authorized by an Organization to have custody," a sweeping catch-all far broader than the enumerated bailees.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: That catch-all overlaps almost exactly with the custodians named in the In Transit definition and hence with Insuring Clause 3, leaving a genuine question of how much of that coverage survives.
judgments.clause_name: Crime 12. Exclusions — (m) custody of bank or armored car

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Any authorized representative of an Insured" is undefined and sits after a specific list of named frauds, and "other fraudulent, dishonest or criminal act" is an open catch-all.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: "Authorized representative" does not map onto either Employee or Third Party as defined, so the exclusion's reach against Insuring Clauses 2-8 is uncertain despite the collusion proviso.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Subparagraph (a) ends with "or other similar representative" after a list of intermediaries — a textbook ejusdem generis question — and (b)(i)-(iii) are otherwise precise.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The catch-all must be reconciled with the Employee definition, which expressly includes leased and temporary workers, creating a plausible overlap dispute.
judgments.clause_name: Crime 13. Exclusions applicable to Insuring Clause 1 or 9

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Both limbs are specific, listing defined perils and identifying the armored-car exception.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cleanly partitions Insuring Clauses 2 and 3 from Clauses 4-8, consistent with Subsection 25's largest-limit rule.
judgments.clause_name: Crime 14. Exclusions applicable to Insuring Clause 2 or 3

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Kidnap, ransom or other extortion payment (as distinct from Robbery)" is defined by contrast and by the threat requirement; reasonably definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Item 3 lists a "Special Coverage" (Kidnap/Ransom forms appear in the Schedule of Forms), so this exclusion is coordinated with a separate section rather than in conflict.
judgments.clause_name: Crime 15. Exclusion — kidnap, ransom or extortion payments

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Registered and coupon obligations are specific instrument types; the clause is narrow and clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Insuring Clause 4 and the Financial Instrument definition.
judgments.clause_name: Crime 16. Exclusion — registered or coupon obligations

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The sixty-day awareness cut-off is quantified, though "an Organization becomes aware" uses a different awareness trigger from the Discovery definition's Executive/Insurance Representative test.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Crime Endorsement No. 4 deletes Exclusion 17 outright, so the quoted text is not operative — a direct clash between the base form and the endorsement.
judgments.clause_name: Crime 17. Exclusion — Computer Fraud after awareness

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Using lowercase "forgery" where the section defines "Forgery" is a drafting slip, and the exclusion appears to swallow the whole of Insuring Clause 8 subject to two conditions.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Because Credit Card Fraud is itself defined as Forgery of a credit-card instrument, this exclusion and Insuring Clause 8 are near-circular and can only be harmonised through the provisos.
judgments.clause_name: Crime 18. Exclusion — credit card written instrument forgery

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The three limbs are quantified and parallel; the sixty-day post-termination notice requirement is definite on its own terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Endorsement No. 3 rewrites Exclusion 19 "in its entirety" to require loss sustained and Discovered before termination with no sixty-day tail, while Endorsement No. 5 also rewrites it "in its entirety" restoring the tail — the base text plus two total replacements leave a genuine unresolved conflict, compounded by Subsection 21(b)'s substitution of one year.
judgments.clause_name: Crime 19. Exclusion — loss sustained and discovered before termination

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The ownership tests are stated precisely, including the Premises-damage and Client provisos.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It addresses Insuring Clauses 1-8 and 9 but says nothing about Insuring Clause 10 expenses, a minor gap rather than a contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The rewrite of Insuring Clause 1 for ERISA Plans and the word-substitution instruction are mechanically clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The substitution operates on "sixty (60) days" in Exclusion 19, but Endorsement No. 3's replacement of Exclusion 19 removes that phrase entirely while Endorsement No. 5 restores it, so this instruction may have nothing to operate on.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Reasonable court costs and attorneys' fees" with a prior-consent requirement is a familiar and workable standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the express carve-back referenced by Exclusion 12(i) and by the suit-limitation provision in Subsection 27(b), so the cross-references align.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The ten-percent revenue test, sixty-day notice period and null-and-void consequence are all precise, though "such information as the Company in its sole discretion may require" is open-ended.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its first paragraph is replaced by Crime Endorsement No. 3 paragraph (2), which shifts the trigger from acquisition date to loss Discovered after that date, so the quoted opening no longer states the operative rule.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The four conditions and the limit-selection rule are set out with unusual precision for a prior-loss clause.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Crime Endorsement No. 3 paragraph (3) deletes Subsection 24 in its entirety along with all references to it, so this provision is wholly displaced — the clearest relational problem in the document alongside the Exclusion 19 tangle.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The per-Insuring-Clause single-loss aggregation rules are repetitive but definite, and "any series of related acts" is the only soft phrase.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its opening words "Subject to Subsection 24" survive in the base form although Endorsement 3 deletes Subsection 24, and Endorsement 3 paragraph (4) replaces the first paragraph with a differently framed sustained/Discovered test — leaving competing versions to reconcile.
judgments.clause_name: Crime 25. Limits of Liability and Retention

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Both non-accumulation sentences are stated in absolute, quantifiable terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Subsection 25's limits and with the deleted prior-loss provision's anti-stacking language.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Earliest practicable moment" plus outer limits of ninety days and six months, and the two-year suit bar, are concretely fixed; the inventory-comparison rule is detailed.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The condition-precedent notice duty must be read against Endorsement No. 1's prejudice requirement for late notice of a Claim, and against General Condition 5's excuse clause, which soften it in ways not cross-referenced here.
judgments.clause_name: Crime 27. Proof of Loss and Legal Proceedings

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The valuation formulas are precise, though "Lost Instrument Bond" is capitalised yet nowhere defined in the section.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supersedes General Condition 6's exchange-rate date, which that condition expressly permits ("except as otherwise provided in any coverage section").

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A four-tier waterfall stated in ordinal terms; unambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the subrogation clause and with the retention scheme in Subsection 25.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Null and void to the extent of the amount recoverable or received" is internally awkward — recoverable but unrecovered insurance could defeat coverage — and "valid and collectible" adds a further judgment call.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps Exclusion 12(m)(ii)'s other-insurance proviso, and the two express the excess principle in different words without cross-reference.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single-word addition ("trustee") stated as a complete replacement of subparagraph (a); mechanically clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supersedes c069 cleanly and creates no tension with the Employee or Discovery definitions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Boilerplate; nothing to construe.

judgments.clause_name: Crime Endorsement No. 1 — headings and unchanged terms

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Exclusion 12.(b) is deleted" is as definite as drafting gets.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It removes the base-form trade-secret exclusion and substitutes the paragraph 2 exclusions, so the printed base text at c091 and this instruction must be read together — clear in direction.
judgments.clause_name: Crime Endorsement/Rider No. 2 — deletion of Exclusion 12.(b)

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Each limb uses "including, but not limited to" followed by a list ending in "any similar type of nonpublic information," a double catch-all whose reach is genuinely uncertain, and "loss involving the disclosure" is broad.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The proviso preserves only Insuring Clause 6, which cuts against Insuring Clause 5's Computer Fraud coverage for the very kind of email-based loss the section otherwise seems to cover — a live tension with the coverage grant.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The substituted paragraph is clear in shifting the coverage trigger to loss "Discovered after the effective date" of acquisition.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It leaves the remaining paragraphs of Subsection 23 (with their acquisition-date null-and-void rule) intact, so the two halves of the amended provision use different reference points.

judgments.reasoning_cat2: The base text of Subsection 25 still opens "Subject to Subsection 24," which this clause purports to delete, so the reader must apply the sweep to make the section coherent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The single substituted sentence — loss sustained before termination and Discovered during the Policy Period — is definite.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Boilerplate; nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its "all other terms unchanged" wording is what leaves the competing Exclusion 19 rewrites both nominally in force, but the clause itself is standard.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line deletion; entirely definite.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Boilerplate; nothing to construe.
